title: 16 — Design a Proximity Service (Yelp / "nearby places")
html:
16 — Design a Proximity Service (Yelp / "nearby places")

The one idea: a 2-D "find everything within r km" query can't use an ordinary index efficiently. Geospatial indexes — geohash, quadtree, S2 — map 2-D space onto 1-D keys so nearby points share prefixes. The data is read-heavy and changes slowly, so the whole index fits in memory and replicates easily.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Return businesses near a user's location within a radius (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 20 km).
  • Business owners add/update/delete businesses — changes needn't be real-time (next day is fine).
  • View business details.
  • 100M DAU, 200M businesses; low latency; privacy (location data).

Estimates: 5 searches/user/day → 100M × 5 ÷ 10^5 ≈ 5,000 search QPS.

Step 2 — High-level design

API

GET /v1/search/nearby?latitude=..&longitude=..&radius=5000   → paginated businesses
GET|POST|PUT|DELETE /v1/businesses/{id}

---
title: Proximity service — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    U["User"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
    LB -->|"/search/nearby"| LBS["Location-based service<br/>(read-only, stateless)"]
    LB -->|"/businesses"| BS["Business service"]
    LBS --> R[("DB replicas<br/>+ geo index")]
    BS --> P[("Primary DB")]
    P -. replication .-> R
    BS --> C[("Cache<br/>business details")]
  • LBS — read-heavy, no writes, stateless → scale horizontally.
  • Business service — low write QPS, higher read QPS for details.
  • Primary/replica DB; replica lag is fine (next-day updates).

Step 3 — Deep dive: geospatial indexing

3.1 Why not two indexes?

WHERE lat BETWEEN a AND b AND lng BETWEEN c AND d — each index returns a huge band; the intersection is expensive. We need a single index over 2-D.

3.2 Options

Approach Idea Notes
Even grid Fixed-size cells Business density is wildly uneven → some cells empty, some overloaded
Geohash Recursively split the world into quadrants, interleave lat/lng bits, base32-encode Nearby places share a prefix; easy to store in any DB / Redis
Quadtree Recursively split a quadrant until each leaf has ≤ k businesses (e.g. 100) Adapts to density; in-memory tree built at startup
Google S2 Map the sphere onto a Hilbert curve, cells at 30 levels Precise region covering, geofencing; more complex

3.3 Geohash

Precision vs radius:

Geohash length Cell size (approx) Use for radius
4 39 km × 19.5 km 20 km
5 4.9 km × 4.9 km 2–5 km
6 1.2 km × 0.6 km 0.5–1 km

Boundary issues:

  1. Two very close points on either side of a cell boundary may share no prefix.
  2. Search the cell plus its 8 neighbours, not only the user's cell.

If too few results: drop one character (bigger cells) and search again.

Storage: geohash_index(geohash, business_id) — one row per business per precision, or a composite key. Plain B-tree index on geohash with LIKE 'prefix%' works.

3.4 Quadtree

  • Built in memory at server startup: 200M businesses → ~2M leaves, a few GB of RAM — fits on one server; replicate for QPS.
  • Search: find the leaf for the user, then expand to neighbours until enough results.
  • Build takes minutes → rolling restarts; incremental updates are fiddly (locking) — acceptable with next-day freshness.

3.5 Geohash vs quadtree

Geohash Quadtree
Where it lives Any DB / Redis In-memory structure
Density adaptation No (fixed cells) Yes
Updates Easy (row insert/delete) Harder (tree rebalancing)
k-nearest Awkward Natural

3.6 Scaling the data

  • Business table: shard by business_id.
  • Geo index: small (a few GB) → don't shard; replicate read replicas to match QPS.
  • Cache: geohash → [business_id] at each precision, and business_id → details.

3.7 Final flow

  1. Client sends lat/lng + radius.
  2. LBS picks geohash precision from radius.
  3. Compute the cell + 8 neighbours.
  4. For each, get business IDs from Redis (geohash → ids).
  5. Fetch details, compute exact distance, rank, paginate.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Multi-region deployment (users close to their data; also helps data-residency law), filters (open now, category), and precision tuning by density.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • SQL Server / Azure SQL geography type with a spatial index: WHERE Location.STDistance(@point) <= @radius — the managed answer for moderate scale. EF Core supports it via NetTopologySuite (UseNetTopologySuite()).
  • Cosmos DB geospatial queries (ST_DISTANCE, ST_WITHIN) with a spatial index on GeoJSON points.
  • Azure Cache for Redis: GEOADD / GEOSEARCH key FROMLONLAT lng lat BYRADIUS 5 km ASC COUNT 20 — geohash under the hood.
  • Azure AI Search: geo.distance() filters and sorting.
  • Azure Maps for geocoding and map rendering.

Review checklist

  • Explain why a 2-D range query needs a special index.
  • Geohash with precision table and neighbour search.
  • Quadtree as the density-adaptive alternative.
  • Replicate the index rather than shard it.
  • Read path with cache.
